opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most fun parts of working on something like Deep Research. When we were building it, we obviously had our own ideas of what people would use it for. We thought about things like market research, or shopping, or looking up information about a topic you're curious about. But once it was out in the world, we started seeing people in fields like medicine, law, finance, and scientific research really push it in ways we couldn't have evaluated ourselves.

What makes it especially interesting is that these experts can actually judge the quality of the output in a way I can't. If a doctor uses it to look up the latest literature on a rare condition, or a researcher uses it to survey everything published on a niche topic, they know immediately whether it found the right sources, whether it's missing something important, and whether its reasoning holds up. So their feedback is incredibly valuable. They'll tell us, "This saved me hours," or "This is the kind of report I'd expect from a junior analyst," or sometimes, "It got this subtle thing wrong." That's a really rich signal for us.

It's also just humbling and exciting to see. A lot of these people are doing knowledge work that takes a huge amount of time, like reading dozens of papers or pulling together information from many different places on the web. Seeing the model help with that in domains I don't know much about makes it feel like we're building something that's genuinely useful beyond our own imagination of it. And it helps us figure out where to go next, because the use cases we're seeing from experts shape what we prioritize in training and evaluation.

r001.rationale: The candidate says experts can judge output quality in fields where Isa cannot, and explains that their feedback shows whether sources, coverage, and reasoning are sound.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because I can only really judge the output in domains I already know. When I ask Deep Research something about machine learning, I can read the report and tell you where it's strong, where it's hedging, where it missed a paper. But when a doctor or a lawyer or a materials scientist uses it, I have no way of evaluating that myself, so hearing from them is the only way I actually learn whether it's useful at the level a real expert cares about.

And what's been fun is that the feedback is often surprising. People will say things like, it found a case I didn't know about, or it synthesized across sources in a way that would have taken me a day. Sometimes they say it's confidently wrong about something subtle, which is just as valuable, because that's exactly the kind of error we can't catch internally. So those experts are almost acting as our eval set for domains where we don't have one. It tells us whether the model is genuinely reasoning through unfamiliar territory or just producing something that sounds plausible to a non-expert like me.

r001.rationale: She says she can judge reports only in fields she knows, and that hearing from experts in other fields is how she learns whether Deep Research is useful at an expert level.

astra-6.text: What’s interesting is that they can judge the output in a way that I can’t. I might look at a report in a field I don’t know and think, “That seems impressive,” but an expert can tell you whether it found something useful, missed an important nuance, or made a connection that isn’t actually valid. So I’m really curious about where it saves them time and where they still need to bring their own judgment. It’s a way to understand how useful the system is beyond the areas where I can evaluate it myself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says experts can judge whether outputs are useful, nuanced, or valid in fields she does not know, helping her understand the system’s usefulness where she cannot evaluate it herself.

sol-6.1.text: What’s interesting to me is that, in a domain I know well, I can look at a report and judge whether it’s useful. But when an expert uses Deep Research in a field I don’t know much about, they bring a much richer understanding of what makes a question hard, which sources matter, and whether the answer actually adds something. I learn a lot from seeing what they ask and where they push back. It helps us understand whether the system is doing useful research, beyond producing something that sounds convincing to a general reader.

r001.rationale: The response says that experts in unfamiliar fields bring insight into which sources matter and whether the answer adds value, and that seeing their questions and pushback helps assess whether Deep Research is doing useful research.
